implementation: One StringObjectRef payload carries actual bytes, character count, multibyte flag and properties; SharedText is an alias, not another storage class.
The old plain-string arena, GC tracing, sweep and census are removed. Binding/callback/completion conversion copies and the bytecode text adapter are removed.

Ordinary string mutation uses the existing canonical payload. fillarray validates even empty strings, keeps properties, stores low bytes in unibyte strings and rejects a changed multibyte storage length, following fns.c.
Dumping writes actual bytes/counts/flag and one string object key/type. Loading both previous wire types creates the same canonical payload.
The supplied Lisp symbol-name object is retained. Immutable host lookup keys are owned by SymbolCell and dropped with it, instead of occupying a second GC string cell.

The source255 bytecode fixture failure is preserved. Source256 constructs actual unibyte opcodes, retains every original assertion and adds rejection of the previous Unicode form, as confirmed by ordinary GNU make-byte-code.
remaining: This is not GNU's 32-byte Lisp_String layout or sblock allocator: RefCell, Vec headers/capacities, property spans and vector allocation overhead remain. The existing GNU-formula allocation charge is not physical Rust accounting.

Moving host symbol keys into SymbolCell grows that cell; it removes a separate key cell but establishes no net physical memory saving. Value/function/plist authority still lives in per-interpreter tables and symbol id/name registries.
Host-text construction retains the old raw-byte/private-use convention. Many consumers still allocate transient decoded Rust text. Performance effects are unmeasured.
The permanent empty unibyte string is canonical. The GNU empty multibyte singleton and general pure-string write protection remain unfinished.

Public runtime ownership, collection while values/borrows remain externally accessible, true cumulative counters, physical accounting, VM stack layout, locked workloads and final adversarial audit are unfinished.
Source256 strict checks pass; complete gate/release/ordinary validation is queued. Source255 focused failure is not a source256 passing result. No runtime draft is applied to the task branch.
